sections.overview: The garden spider, also called cross spider or diadem spider, is a familiar orb-weaving spider. It is most noticeable in autumn, when full-grown females sit at the centre of their wheel-shaped webs. Hatching in spring, it usually matures the following summer, and the females die before the new year after laying their eggs.
sections.identification: Males measure 4–8 mm and females 10–18 mm in body length; another source gives up to 20 mm for females. The abdomen has ‘shoulders’, so it is wider at the front, and ranges from pale straw to dark brown or reddish with a darker central pattern holding white markings that can form a cross. The legs are banded brown and carry many short spines. A reliable species-wide adult body-mass range was not found in the consulted sources; spider mass varies with sex, age and feeding condition.
sections.habitat: In Britain it is probably the most common and widespread large spider, found in gardens, hedges, fences, scrub, woodland edges and heathland. It needs supports to anchor its web, up to about two metres above the ground, and is rarely found indoors, probably because houses are too dry. It has also been recorded across the northern United States.
sections.diet: It feeds on insects and other arthropods caught in its web. When prey struggles in the sticky spiral, the spider rushes over, wraps it in swathes of silk and bites it. The wrapped prey may be eaten at once or kept for later.
sections.behavior: The spider builds its orb web in about half an hour, using only the sense of touch, with roughly 25 to 30 radial threads. Because dust and pollen soon dull the sticky droplets, it rebuilds the web every day or so and eats the old one to recycle the silk proteins. It usually hangs head down at the hub and, if disturbed, shakes the web to a blur.
sections.reproduction: Spiderlings leave the egg sac in May and cluster in a golden ball, then disperse after about a week. They overwinter half-grown, males mature in August or September and females a couple of weeks later, though in southern Britain some mature in their first year. A male announces himself by plucking the female’s web; the female lays her eggs in a sheltered spot inside a yellowish silk sac, guards it and dies before the new year.
sections.ecology: As a predator of flying insects the garden spider can help limit pest numbers. Mating is risky for the male, who must signal that he is a suitor and not a meal. Young spiders disperse by ballooning, drifting on silk threads carried by the wind.
sections.conservation: No threat is reported for this common species. Animal Diversity Web lists it with no special status, but that account is not a current global assessment and no recent Red List category was read. In Britain it is among the most frequently recorded large spiders.
